div.head: Letter to the Editor
div.p: Canines with different pathologies as carriers of diverse lineages of Escherichia coli harbouring mcr-1 and clinically relevant β-lactamases in central Ecuador

div.head: Sir,
div.p: It has been considered that companion animals may act as reservoirs for pathogenic bacteria, which is a major concern considering that inadequate management of animal waste or cross-contact may represent potential transmission routes of pathogenic bacteria, including their antimicrobial resistance genes [1]. In this study, we report the presence and diversity of Escherichia coli strains harbouring mcr-1 and clinically relevant β-lactamases isolated from dogs in Ambato, central Ecuador, during 2018.

A total of 117 faecal samples were collected between December 2017 and May 2018 from three veterinary hospitals and three stray dog rescue facilities. Collection of samples was based on the owner's willingness to collaborate in this study. A standardised questionnaire was used to collect animal information. Single colonies with E. coli-like morphology isolated from faecal samples were confirmed using biochemical tests. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing was performed using VITEK(2 and the broth microdilution method for colistin according to Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI) guidelines.

Phenotypic extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL), serine carbapenemase and metallo-β-lactamase production was evaluated by double-disc synergy tests. Isolates were screened by PCR and sequencing analysis for the presence of genes conferring resistance to colistin (mcr-1), β-lactams (bla OXA-48 , bla VIM , bla KPC , bla NDM , bla IMI , bla IMP , bla TEM , bla CTX-M groups 1, 2, 8, 9 and 25 , bla SHV and bla CMY ), tetracycline (tetA) and sulfonamides (sul1) using the primers listed in Supplementary Table S1.

The sequence type (ST) of mcr-1-positive E. coli isolates was identified by multilocus sequence typing (MLST) according to the database of the Center for Genomic Epidemiology. Pulsed-field gel electrophoresis (PFGE) was performed using the restriction enzyme XbaI. Comparison of PFGE patterns was performed with GelJ software v.2.0 using the Dice similarity coefficient. Clusters were defined as DNA patterns sharing >85% similarity. Finally, to characterise plasmids related to the mcr-1 gene, PCR-based replicon typing (PBRT) was performed.

The results revealed that only 3 of the 117 isolates were positive for mcr-1 (strains UTA-028, UTA-069 and UTA-103), all of which were from veterinary hospital dogs. Escherichia coli UTA-028 was isolated from a dog with canine gastroenteritis (a 1-month-old male Shi Tzu) and was resistant to ceftriaxone and ciprofloxacin. In contrast, E. coli UTA-069 was isolated from a dog with canine distemper (a 6-month-old female Cocker Spaniel) and showed resistance to ceftriaxone, ceftazidime, ampicillin/sulbactam and ciprofloxacin. Furthermore, E. coli UTA-103 was isolated from an animal with no clinical signs of disease (an 8-year-old male mixedbreed) and showed resistance to ceftriaxone, ampicillin/sulbactam, gentamicin and ciprofloxacin (Table 1).

Based on MLST, E. coli strains UTA-028, UTA-069 and UTA-103 belonged to ST162, ST1196 and ST744, respectively. The ST162 and ST1196 isolates harboured bla CTX-M-55 , whilst the ST744 isolate harboured bla CTX-M-65 . None of the 117 isolates collected were positive for carbapenemase genes. PFGE results revealed two different patterns between strains UTA-069 and UTA-103. Strain UTA-028 could not be typed via PFGE either due to bacterial lysis problems or DNA digestion (Supplementary Fig. S1).

The three strains successfully transferred the mcr-1 gene to E. coli J53, indicating its plasmid origin (Table 1; Supplementary Table S2). Different types of plasmids were found by PBRT. Strains UTA-028 and UTA-069 shared IncFIIS and IncFII plasmids, and all three strains shared an IncI 2 replicon-type plasmid. Unfortunately, despite our efforts, we could not determine which plasmid carried the mcr-1 gene.

In general terms, the occurrence of mcr-1-containing E. coli isolates was low relative compared with the occurrence in domestic animals in other countries [2]. Some authors suggest that the occurrence of this gene in domestic animals might be related to the consumption of animal-origin food [3]. In the current study, there was a notable difference in terms of clonal diversity in these isolates. Regarding the detected ESBL genes (bla CTX-M-55 and bla CTX-M-65 ), they have been found frequently in E. coli of human and animal origin in Ecuador [4,5]. All of the strains mentioned in this study harboured IncI 2 -type plasmids, which are commonly linked to carriage of the mcr-1 gene [2]. This observation suggests that acquisition of the mcr-1 gene by bacteria from domestic animals poses a threat considering their ability for horizontal gene transfer. Colistin is not commonly used in the treatment of domestic animals, therefore the means of colistin resistance acquisition in these strains was from an external source. The presence of multidrug-resistant (MDR) mcr-1-carrying E. coli in dogs with different clinical diagnoses is worrisome and suggests that pets might represent a silent reservoir of MDR bacteria. These findings highlight the importance of properly managing pet waste and suggest that interactions between people and their pets should be modified in some circumstances.
